description: We are two high school students wanting to build the lunar landing site navigator challenge. If anyone is technical, they can join our team.
summary: Lunar Window is a web mission explorer for the lunar south pole. A planner picks a place (Connecting Ridge or Shackleton Rim), a UTC arrival time and a duration of up to 168 hours, then sees how terrain controls sunlight and Earth contact, and what a schedule slip costs. We built it from actual NASA LOLA elevation data and JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions on a one-minute grid (14 Nov to 15 Dec 2026). A rotatable 3D terrain view, a moment-by-moment panel (Sun elevation, share of the Sun's disc clearing the horizon, Earth elevation) and a ±72-hour arrival chart answer the question planners actually ask: "if we land later, what do we lose?" For example: delaying a Connecting Ridge landing by 48 hours drops nominal Sun exposure from 67.1 to 27.2 equivalent full-Sun hours, and the app states which targets are met, missed or uncertain. It is built to be honest: terrain out to 300 km, finite sensitivity ranges, no invented imagery, missing data left unknown, and limits stated plainly. It matters because polar light is brief and fragmented, so power and communication budgets hinge on timing. Lunar Window turns raw NASA data into a decision a planner can inspect.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Window follows one decision flow: choose a place, inspect terrain and visibility, compare an arrival-time change.

1) Choose a place. Pick Connecting Ridge or Shackleton Rim, a UTC arrival, and 1-168 hours. A rotatable 3D terrain view is drawn from NASA LOLA elevation (64 x 64 km polar region, or the 16 x 16 km study-point tile). A contour map and a month strip show each point's recorded Sun and Earth visibility across the whole dataset.

2) See the visibility. Play or scrub the sampled Sun/Earth record. An "At this moment" panel gives solar elevation, how much of the Sun's disc clears the terrain, Earth's elevation and time to the next change. The terrain is lit from the recorded Sun direction. A skyline diagram shows both bodies against the 300 km terrain horizon, and a text view gives the same reading for screen-reader users.

3) Compare the plan. Change the arrival time while location and duration stay fixed. One sentence names every target that is met, missed, uncertain or unavailable. A chart re-evaluates the mission at every whole-hour arrival from 72 h earlier to 72 h later, and a bounded search checks recovery options across both sites.

WORKED EXAMPLE

Connecting Ridge, arrival 22 Nov 2026 00:00 UTC, 72 hours: 67.12 equivalent full-Sun hours. Arriving 48 hours later: 27.19, a loss of 39.93 hours. A 24-hour delay is flagged uncertain, because the tested range (32.6-61.2 h) straddles the 48-hour example target. In the arrival chart, 81 of 145 whole-hour arrivals meet all three example targets, 29 are uncertain and 35 miss at least one.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Landing windows near the lunar south pole are set by terrain shadowing as much as by orbital geometry. Planners need to know how much sunlight and Earth line-of-sight a place gets over a mission, and how fast that degrades if the schedule moves. Lunar Window makes that trade visible, quickly and with its uncertainty shown. It is a decision-support tool for early mission planning, education and public outreach. It works offline from bundled data: no API key, account or backend.

HOW IT WORKS (SCIENCE)

- Terrain: NASA LOLA 5 m site products for Connecting Ridge (Site01) and Shackleton Rim (Site04), plus 20/80/240 m regional products, form a near-to-far hierarchy out to 300 km. The observer sits 2 m above the registered terrain.

- Sky: JPL Horizons supplies apparent Sun and Earth directions and angular diameters from each site on a one-minute grid (44,641 samples per body per site), 14 Nov-15 Dec 2026.

- Visibility: lunar curvature is modeled in 3-D. A conservative analytic skyline (0.05-degree bins, never smoothed downward) is compared with the Sun's disc using spherical-cap bounds and Gauss-Legendre quadrature. Sun exposure integrates the visible fraction of the solar disc, so half a Sun for two hours counts as one full-Sun hour. Earth visibility uses center clearance.

- Uncertainty: ten finite sensitivity experiments (horizontal shifts, observer-height changes, finer/coarser skyline and mesh, extent) give outer bounds. If a target falls inside the range, the app says "uncertain" instead of guessing.

- Validation: 83 JavaScript tests, 70 Python tests, a 27-asset SHA256 manifest, and a 19-check real-browser journey test. An independent SPICE cross-check (SpiceyPy, DE440s) agrees with Horizons to 0.049 arcseconds across 32 epochs. A conditional far-field audit tests the 300 km cutoff.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

React 19, TypeScript and Vite for the app, with WebGL for the terrain stage. Python (NumPy, rasterio, pyproj, SpiceyPy) runs the offline data pipeline. Playwright runs the browser checks. IBM Plex fonts (OFL). All shipped data is hashed and reproducible from the included scripts.

CREATIVITY

Most lunar tools show a map or a light model. Lunar Window ties them to a mission decision: arrival-time sweeps, a plain-language verdict, and uncertainty-aware targets. Every pixel of the terrain view comes from NASA elevation, with no textures, no procedural craters and no photographs. Shading is computed from elevation alone, and the interface labels it as elevation, not imagery.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty above polish. Equivalent Sun hours are not generated electricity. Earth visibility does not guarantee a radio link. The study points are published region centers, not certified touchdown sites. Sensitivity ranges are not statistical confidence intervals. Physical illumination validation, correlated DEM error and sub-grid terrain remain open and are documented in docs/SCIENCE.md. Targets are user-adjustable examples, not NASA requirements.

Code and documentation: https://github.com/TanujBuilds/lunar-window
